steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper studying how model compression (pruning, quantization) and low data volume affect transferring pre-trained models with visual prompting, including the effect on calibration. Set up the transfer learning background, the gap we address, our study design, and a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- From task-specific training to foundation models; transfer by LP and FF
- Visual prompting / model reprogramming as an alternative
- Gap: LP vs VP under low data and compression; hidden costs of compressed models
- Study design: few-shot settings, many sparse and quantized models
- Calibration of compressed models transferred with VP
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - deep learning: task-specific models -> extensive task-agnostic pre-training
  - goal: robust universal representations, many downstream tasks without intensive training; "Foundation models" (FM) (cite)
  - efficacy shown via simple, cheap adaptation, e.g. linear probing (LP) (cite), in transfer learning
  - transfer learning historically: full fine-tuning (FF) and LP
  - FF generally better but costly; LP cheaper, typically lower performance
- Visual prompting
  - model reprogramming (cite) / visual prompting (VP) (cite): viable, efficient alternative, rivals LP in performance and transfer cost
  - learn a perturbation applied to target inputs so pre-trained model classifies "reprogrammed" sample correctly, weights unchanged
  - aligns target features with source features, no gradient updates to weights -> competes with LP on efficiency
- Gap
  - studies evaluate LP and VP across target data scenarios (cite)
  - little exploration of differences under (a) low data volume and (b) model compression
  - aim: hidden costs of compressed models in transfer learning across data volume settings
  - known costs: reliability (cite), distribution shift performance (cite), fairness (cite), more
- Study design
  - low data volume: few-shot transferability
  - compression: sparse and quantized models from unstructured pruning (cite), structural pruning (cite), quantization (cite), Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) (cite)
- Calibration
  - effect of transferring compressed models with VP on calibration in target task vs dense counterparts
  - recent research: fairness and reliability (cite), pruning strategies and resulting models (cite)
  - gap: reliability of VP as adaptation mechanism across compression rates
- Contributions
  - 1. empirical study: compression + low data volume on transferability via VP
  - 2. eight datasets: compressed models notably worse than dense via VP
  - 3. sparse models hurt calibration after VP transfer; first exploration
  - 4. quantized models do not suffer calibration harm; intuitive analysis
  - 5. fine-grained overview by compression method category, Table 1
  - 6. differences in visual prompts and label mapping learned by compressed vs dense full-precision models

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning has moved from training task-specific models to extensive task-agnostic pre-training. The goal is to build a model with robust universal representations that can be used for many downstream tasks without intensive training. These kinds of models are now called "Foundation models" (FM). How well these pre-trained models work for downstream tasks has often been shown with simple and computationally efficient adaptation methods, like linear probing (LP), as part of the broader framework of transfer learning. Transfer learning has traditionally been the basic way to adapt pre-trained models to different downstream tasks, and historically it was limited to full fine-tuning (FF) and LP. FF usually performs better but it is also the more costly approach, while LP is computationally cheaper but usually performs worse than full fine-tuning.

LP and FF have been the standard transfer learning methods, but a new approach has appeared, called model reprogramming or, more commonly, visual prompting (VP). It is a viable and efficient alternative that can rival LP in both performance and transfer cost. Basically, VP learns a perturbation so that when it is applied to the input samples of the target dataset, the pre-trained model classifies the resulting "reprogrammed" sample correctly, without changing the weights at all. Reprogramming works by aligning the features of the target data with the features of the source data, so there is no need for gradient updates to the network weights. Because of this, VP often competes with LP on efficiency.

Several studies in the literature have empirically evaluated how LP and VP perform across different target data scenarios, but there has not been much exploration of how the two methods differ under the constraints of (a) low data volume and (b) model compression. In this study we want to reveal the hidden costs of compressed models in transfer learning across different data volume settings. In the existing literature these costs cover a broad range of model attributes, like reliability, performance under distribution shifts, fairness, and more.

- Study design
  - low data volume: few-shot transferability
  - compression: sparse and quantized models via unstructured pruning, structural pruning, quantization, LTH-based solutions
- Calibration: effect of VP transfer of compressed models on target calibration vs dense; prior work on fairness/reliability and on pruning strategies; gap = reliability of VP across compression rates
- Contributions
  - 1. empirical study of compression + low data on VP transferability
  - 2. eight datasets: compressed notably worse than dense
  - 3. sparse models hurt calibration after VP transfer (first exploration)
  - 4. quantized models don't; intuitive analysis
  - 5. overview by compression category, Table 1
  - 6. visual prompts and label mapping: compressed vs dense full-precision

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning has moved from training task-specific models to extensive task-agnostic pre-training. The goal is to build a model with robust universal representations that can be used for many downstream tasks without intensive training. These kinds of models are now called "Foundation models" (FM). How well these pre-trained models work for downstream tasks has often been shown with simple and computationally efficient adaptation methods, like linear probing (LP), as part of the broader framework of transfer learning. Transfer learning has traditionally been the basic way to adapt pre-trained models to different downstream tasks, and historically it was limited to full fine-tuning (FF) and LP. FF usually performs better but it is also the more costly approach, while LP is computationally cheaper but usually performs worse than full fine-tuning.

LP and FF have been the standard transfer learning methods, but a new approach has appeared, called model reprogramming or, more commonly, visual prompting (VP). It is a viable and efficient alternative that can rival LP in both performance and transfer cost. Basically, VP learns a perturbation so that when it is applied to the input samples of the target dataset, the pre-trained model classifies the resulting "reprogrammed" sample correctly, without changing the weights at all. Reprogramming works by aligning the features of the target data with the features of the source data, so there is no need for gradient updates to the network weights. Because of this, VP often competes with LP on efficiency.

Several studies in the literature have empirically evaluated how LP and VP perform across different target data scenarios, but there has not been much exploration of how the two methods differ under the constraints of (a) low data volume and (b) model compression. In this study we want to reveal the hidden costs of compressed models in transfer learning across different data volume settings. In the existing literature these costs cover a broad range of model attributes, like reliability, performance under distribution shifts, fairness, and more.

For the low data volume constraint, we look at the transferability of pre-trained models in few-shot settings. For the model compression constraint, we look at a wide range of sparse and quantized models produced by compression techniques like unstructured pruning, structural pruning, quantization, and solutions based on the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH).

We also extend our empirical framework to look at how transferring compressed models with VP affects the calibration of the resulting model on the target task, compared to the dense counterparts. Recent research has focused on understanding and improving fairness and reliability in models, and also on examining pruning strategies and the models they produce, but we still do not understand well how reliable visual prompting is as an adaptation mechanism, especially when the model compression rate varies.

Our main contributions are:

1. We do a comprehensive empirical investigation of how model compression and low data volume affect the transferability of pre-trained models with visual prompting methods.

2. Our analysis on eight datasets shows that compressed models perform notably worse than their dense counterparts when transferred with visual prompting.

3. We empirically examine the negative impact of using sparse models on the calibration of the final model we get after transferring to the downstream target task with visual prompting. This is the first exploration of this phenomenon.

4. On the other hand, we show that quantized models do not suffer from the negative effects on calibration that we see in sparse models, and we give an intuitive analysis to explain this.

5. We give a fine-grained overview of our observations, organized by the categories of compression methods, in Table 1.

6. We also give new insights into how the visual prompts and their label mapping learned by compressed models differ from those of their dense, full-precision counterparts.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The evolution of deep learning has shifted from training task-specific models to extensive task-agnostic pre-training. The objective is to construct a model with robust universal representations that facilitates numerous downstream tasks without intensive training. This category of models is now referred to as "Foundation models" (FM) [8]. The efficacy of these pre-trained models for downstream tasks has often been demonstrated through simple and computationally efficient adaptation methods, such as linear probing (LP) [9], within the broader framework of transfer learning. Transfer learning has traditionally been fundamental for adapting pre-trained models to various downstream tasks, and has historically been constrained to full fine-tuning (FF) and LP. The former, while generally superior in performance, is the more costly approach, whereas the latter is computationally cheaper but typically shows lower performance than full fine-tuning.

Although LP and FF have traditionally served as the standard transfer learning methods, a novel approach, referred to as model reprogramming [10,11,12] or more commonly as visual prompting (VP) [13,14,15], has emerged as a viable and efficient alternative, capable of rivaling LP in both performance and transfer cost. Essentially, VP learns a perturbation such that, when applied to input samples of the target dataset, the pre-trained model accurately classifies the resulting "reprogrammed" sample without any changes to the weights. Reprogramming relies on aligning the features of the target data with those of the source data, eliminating the need for gradient updates to the network weights. Consequently, VP often competes with LP in terms of efficiency.

While several studies in the literature have empirically evaluated the performance of LP and VP across diverse target data scenarios [11,13,16,17,18], there has been limited exploration of the differences between the two methods under the constraints of (a) low data volume and (b) model compression. This study aims to reveal the hidden costs of compressed models in transfer learning across various data volume settings. In the existing literature, these costs span a broad spectrum of model attributes, such as reliability [19,20], performance under distribution shifts [21,22], fairness [23,24,25], and more.

To this end, under the constraint of low data volume, we examine the transferability of pre-trained models in few-shot settings. For the constraint of model compression, our investigation covers a wide array of sparse and quantized models generated through compression techniques such as unstructured pruning [26,27,28], structural pruning [29,30], quantization [31,32,33,34,7], and solutions based on the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) [3].

Moreover, we extend our empirical framework to investigate how transferring compressed models using VP influences the calibration of the resulting model in the target task, compared to its dense counterparts. Although recent research has prioritized understanding and improving fairness and reliability in models [15], along with examining pruning strategies and the resulting models [35,36,37,38,39], there remains a gap in our understanding of the reliability of visual prompting as an adaptation mechanism, particularly under varying model compression rates.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows.

- 1. We conduct a comprehensive empirical investigation into the effects of model compression and low data volume on the transferability of pre-trained models through visual prompting methods.

- 2. Our analysis across eight datasets reveals a notable decrease in performance for compressed models compared to their dense counterparts when transferred via visual prompting.

- 3. We empirically examine the adverse impact of using sparse models on the calibration of the final model obtained after transfer to the downstream target task using visual prompting, the first exploration of this phenomenon.

- 4. In contrast, we show that quantized models do not suffer from the adverse effects on calibration observed in sparse models, and offer an intuitive analysis of this phenomenon.

- 5. We provide a fine-grained overview of our observations based on the categorization of different compression methods in Table 1.

- 6. Furthermore, we contribute novel insights into the differences between visual prompts and their corresponding label mapping learned by compressed models and by their dense, full-precision counterparts.
